lectures.title: File Systems Overview and Creating a first Partition

So but, but usually those partitions, they all have a file system to store the data.
A file system is responsible for the data organization, so it's storing the files in folders and files,
and it defines how this should be stored on a physical layer.
It's responsible for space allocation, so it's managing free and the use space and releasing space
when files are deleted.
Maybe they're the for example, on SSDs there is a specific command that can be sent to those SSDs to
let them know that this space now is actually free.
The file system is responsible for that and it helps with wear leveling on the SSD that it gets used,
that the physical bits get used on a in the same way for the whole drive.
So it prevents or it allows a higher lifespan for the SSDs.
A file system is also responsible for the management of metadata, so it's storing permissions, ownerships
timestamps like when have we created a file, when have we updated a file the last time?
So it's responsible for a lot of stuff.
Another thing that's really important is that a file system also takes care of data integrity, so it
usually implements mechanism for error detection on and it's trying to make sure that the file system
is always in a consistent state, preferably even after an unpredicted power loss.
So even if we would just shut off our computer because maybe we have a power outage or something like
that, good file systems would make sure that the file system is still in a consistent state and that
either a file has been fully written or not, but nothing in between.
